# Working in a project with an OpenDomain workspace

This project records what it knows about its domain in `opendomain/`, as linked
Markdown artifacts. The `opendomain` command reads that knowledge and checks the links
between artifacts. It is the authority on what this project has established: if
you want to know whether something here is known, inferred or assumed, ask `opendomain`.

## The one rule

Every artifact declares an `epistemic` value. Use the honest one.

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `EXPLICIT` | A cited source states this directly. Record `derived-from`. |
| `TACIT` | Known by practice, not written anywhere. |
| `HYBRID` | Partly stated, partly practice. |
| `INFERRED` | Derived by reasoning. Write the chain and set `confidence`. |
| `ASSUMED` | Nobody knows yet. Say so in the prose. |
| `UNKNOWN` | A known gap. Track it; do not fill it in. |
| `CONFLICTING` | Sources disagree. Record both, resolve nothing. |

**Never write `EXPLICIT` for something you inferred.** A confident domain rule
built on general knowledge, with no source behind it, is `ASSUMED` with the
reasoning written down. Writing it as `EXPLICIT` is epistemic laundering, and it
is the specific failure this framework exists to catch.

**Never invent a `SRC-` or `EVD-` identifier** to make a claim look sourced. A
fabricated citation is worse than an honest gap: it propagates through every
downstream gate and becomes indistinguishable from a real one. If you could not
find a source, say so.

## Reading and writing artifacts

Each registry is a Markdown file of `##` headings, one per artifact, with a
fenced `toml` block that is machine-checked and prose that is never parsed:

````markdown
## REQ-004 — Reject a receipt exceeding the outstanding quantity

```toml
type = "FUNCTIONAL"
status = "VALIDATED"
epistemic = "EXPLICIT"
derived-from = ["EVD-014", "RULE-001"]
```

**Statement**

The system SHALL reject a goods receipt whose accepted quantity exceeds the
remaining quantity of the referenced purchase order line.
````

A malformed `toml` block is reported with a line number and never guessed at, so
you can write as much prose as the subject deserves without risking a parse
error.

Links are declared by the artifact that depends on the other, not the reverse:
`REQ-004 derived-from RULE-001`, never `RULE-001 derived-from REQ-004`.

Run `opendomain reference` for the identifier prefixes, the relations, and the vocabulary
of statuses and epistemic values. Do not guess a prefix.

## The commands

`opendomain --help` is authoritative. If a command you expected is missing, that is a
fact about the tool, not an invitation to assume it exists.

### Reading

| Question | Command |
|---|---|
| Where does the project stand, and what is blocking? | `opendomain status` |
| Is anything dangling, unjustified or unresolved? | `opendomain audit` |
| Are all declared links resolvable? | `opendomain link --check` |
| What do the identifiers and rules mean? | `opendomain reference` (63 rules, 9 gates, 37 kinds) |
| Give me one artifact in full | `opendomain show <ID>` |
| Why does this artifact exist? | `opendomain trace <ID>` |
| What implements and verifies it? | `opendomain trace <ID> --forward` |
| Who said so, nearest source first? | `opendomain trace <ID> --provenance` |
| What breaks if this changes? | `opendomain impact <ID>` |
| What does the traceability graph look like? | `opendomain graph [--root <ID>] [--depth N] [--dot]` |
| Give the whole knowledge base to a human? | `opendomain export [--format pdf\|html] [--graph mermaid\|dot\|none]` |
| Is it consistent enough to proceed? | `opendomain gate <gate>` |

`opendomain show` prints the record; `opendomain trace` explains it. Reach for `show` when you
want the artifact, and for `trace` when you want the argument for it.

`opendomain graph` renders Mermaid by default and Graphviz DOT under `--dot`. It is
capped at 200 nodes, so a large workspace will be truncated rather than
unreadable; raise `--limit` if you need the whole graph and accept the output.

`opendomain export` mirrors the whole `opendomain/` tree as one paginated document -
a status cover, the traceability graph (Mermaid by default, Graphviz DOT under
`--graph dot`), then every file in gate order, records unfolded as readable
tables. The PDF is printed headlessly by the machine's own browser (Edge or
Chrome are auto-detected; `--browser` or `OPENDOMAIN_BROWSER` pick another);
without one the styled HTML stays instead, and the command says so. The
printout lists the same numbers `status` does; a PDF is a printout, so never
cite it against a registry changed since - rerun the export or read the
registry.

### Checking and writing

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `opendomain init [--name N] [--profile lean\|core\|full]` | Writes `opendomain/` and the agent contract; each generated tree (opendomain/, .opencode/) carries its own `.gitignore` — regenerable like the rest, delete it to version that tree (the registries are the F14/L9 evidence). |
| `opendomain gate <gate>` | Runs one gate. Exits non-zero on a blocking finding. |
| `opendomain gate --through <n>` | Runs every gate up to and including number `n` (0–8). |
| `opendomain link <ID> <relation> <TARGET>` | Records a link declared by the dependent artifact. |
| `opendomain link --check` | Verifies declared links resolve. |
| `opendomain new <KIND> [--scope S]` | Prints the next free identifier of a kind. Read-only; re-run before writing. |
| `opendomain advance <ID> <STATUS>` | Moves an artifact along its lifecycle. |
| `opendomain propose <slug> [--summary S]` | Opens a change proposal under `changes/`. |
| `opendomain apply <slug>` | Marks a change as applied. |
| `opendomain archive <slug>` | Moves a completed change under `changes/archive/`. |

### Verification (Sections 9/10)

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `opendomain rigour` | Prints the Section 9.7 rigour table; audits which requirement records declare a rigour today. |
| `opendomain provision [--dry-run]` | Stack detection (repository-only), the ordered selection rules, then generated `.feature` scaffolds with `@AC` tags and provenance — or a refusal recorded as a DEC artifact. Nothing is installed. |
| `opendomain bind` | Audit of binding provenance (GENERATED/ANNOTATED/ATTRIBUTED/INFERRED) and verification depth (executed/discovered/declared). Findings, not gate rules. |
| `opendomain provenance` | Verifies each record's `run = "…"` citation against the archived run it names — and lists the archives no record claims (F14/L9 bridge). |

Gates are named `context`, `research`, `domain`, `requirements`, `opportunity`,
`specification`, `plan`, `implementation`, `completion`. `opendomain gate <name>` takes
the name; `opendomain gate --through` takes the number (0–8), so `opendomain gate --through 3`
runs every gate up to and including `requirements`. The two are not
interchangeable, and passing a name to `--through` is an error rather than a
silent no-op.

| # | Gate | The question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `context` | Do we know what we are building, and what is already true? |
| 1 | `research` | Is the domain understood well enough to derive requirements? |
| 2 | `domain` | Is the domain model coherent, owned and cross-linked? |
| 3 | `requirements` | Is every requirement justified, testable and traced? |
| 4 | `opportunity` | Has anything been challenged, and is the chosen concept earned? |
| 5 | `specification` | Does the specification describe observable behaviour and nothing else? |
| 6 | `plan` | Is there a bounded, ordered plan that can realise the specification? |
| 7 | `implementation` | Did implementation satisfy the acceptance criteria without drift? |
| 8 | `completion` | Is the whole chain coherent, tested and free of critical unknowns? |

Gates are cumulative: reaching gate 8 means 0 through 7 passed too. Run
`opendomain gate --through 8` to check the whole chain, or `opendomain gate <n>` for one stage.

These gates guard what the project **claims** in its registries: a claim whose
chain is broken is a gate finding, not an opinion. Keep the same discipline in
whatever executes the work — no execution may rewrite a claim without the
evidence its gate requires, and a verification the party it verifies controls
is not a verification: never re-label `ASSUMED` as `EXPLICIT` without
intervening evidence. A `TEST` or `DRIFT` record stores its evidence in the
registries themselves, cited by identifier.

`opendomain reference` lists the **63 rules** these gates apply — 35 blocking, 28
advisory — grouped by gate, and `opendomain reference --json` returns the same list
machine-readably. Read it before you write artifacts rather than after a gate
fails: a rule you learn about by tripping it is a rule that has already cost you
a change.

`opendomain gate --strict` is accepted and changes nothing: a blocking finding always
fails the command and an advisory one never does, regardless of the flag.

`opendomain --json` works on every command, for a machine-readable result instead of a
rendered one. `-C <dir>` points any command at another project.

`opendomain propose`, `opendomain apply` and `opendomain archive` manage a change through the OpenSpec
layout: propose it, implement it, apply it, archive it. An agent working a task
should propose rather than edit registries directly, so that what changed and why
is recorded as a change rather than as an unexplained diff.

Only `init`, `link`, `advance`, `propose`, `apply`, `archive` and `export` write -
and `export` writes its own output file only. Every other command only reads, and
reads the registries as they are.

### When the work must be executed by agents

The door is one: `/opendomain-harness` (opencode) routes to the
`opendomain-harness` agent — the execution architect. A `TASK-###` record
becomes a planned, grounded and gated agent system; a finished or failed run
is recovered (`verify`, `attribute`, `resume`, `repatch`), never re-run
blind. Every implementation executed by agents goes through this verified
harness; evidence is archived under `opendomain/harness/runs/` and cited
`run = "…"`, then checked by `opendomain provenance`. There is no
free-standing implementer to call.

Roles and skills are different objects, and their names are not interchangeable.
The three roles (`context-completer`, `domain-researcher`, `opendomain-harness`)
live in `.opencode/agent/` and are invoked with the subagent tool
(`agent: "<role name>"`) or through the slash command that routes to them;
they are never loaded through the skill tool. The skills live in
`.opencode/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and are loaded by exact directory name —
including `context-completer`, the Phase 0 doctrine of the interviewer role.
No skill named `opendomain-context-completer` exists, and no other name that
merely sounds plausible does either: when a skill fails to load, the reason is
a wrong name, and the correction is to check the index
(`.opencode/skills/opendomain/SKILL.md`) rather than to try variants. The same
applies to commands and agent identifiers: aliases are not inferred, they are
read where they are declared.

## Gates are not a formality

A gate failure is a finding with a stable rule slug, such as
`gate-3/unjustified-requirement`, and a failing gate exits non-zero so it works
as a CI step.

Findings come in two severities. **Blocking** means the stage produced nothing
usable, and `opendomain gate` exits non-zero. **Advisory** means a rule of discipline was
broken that does not make the output unusable; it is reported and recorded, and
it does not fail the command. Neither is negotiable at the call site: an agent
cannot decide a finding is advisory, and `--strict` does not change it.

Report a failure as a failure. Do not describe a blocking finding as advisory
because the surrounding work looks finished, and do not edit an artifact to
silence a finding — an artifact edited to quiet a gate is the laundering the
framework detects, performed by you.

## Recording how a claim got stronger

When an artifact's status moves to `VALIDATED` or `VERIFIED`, record the move:

```toml
promotions = [
  { from = "ASSUMED", to = "VALIDATED", evidence = ["EVD-014"], date = "2026-04-10" }
]
```

Without that record, a change of epistemic state and a change of status are
indistinguishable from each other. A promotion that cites no evidence, cites an
identifier that does not exist, or cites evidence that is not itself `EXPLICIT`
is a blocking finding.

## Before you finish

Run `opendomain link --check` and `opendomain gate <current-gate>`, then report what they say.
When a gate fails, say it fails.

# Completing project context

The role `context-completer` (`.opencode/agent/context-completer.md`) owns Phase 0. This skill is the same doctrine in loadable form: when the role can be spawned, delegate to it — the `subagent` tool with `agent: "context-completer"`, or `/opendomain-project`, which does exactly that. When no subagent can be spawned, do the work yourself under these rules, never under invented ones.

## One name, exactly

The skill's loadable name is `context-completer` — the role's name, without a prefix. There is no `opendomain-context-completer` skill and never was: a failed load under that name is a wrong name, not a missing file. The emitted skills are listed in the index `.opencode/skills/opendomain/SKILL.md`; read it instead of trying variants that sound plausible.

## Phase 1 — read the repository first

Read what actually exists, citing `path:line` for every fact — identity, languages and frameworks, services and entry points, the data model, the documentation, the conventions visible in git history, whatever context is already recorded. Stay out of target, node_modules and build directories. Note secret paths and key names, never values.

## Phase 2 — research the outside through the researcher

Pull 5–12 keywords — domain nouns, the suspected jurisdiction, the stack, any regulation glimpsed in code — and delegate each direction to `domain-researcher`; when that role cannot be spawned, search it yourself one direction at a time, in parallel. Regulation, official documentation, industry practice, competitors as clues. Fold findings into your work when they return, and never record on the researcher's behalf.

## Phase 3 — write the context honestly

Fill every section of `project.md`, copy the essence into short `[project]` strings in `opendomain.toml`, and create `DOM-001`/`STK-001` only when the registry holds none yet — anything already written stays untouched. What you read in code is `INFERRED`; what comes from speech or general knowledge is `ASSUMED`; `EXPLICIT` requires a source you read, linked. Holes become tracked uncertainties; working hypotheses get dated; disagreements become unsettled conflicts.

## Phase 4 — ask what no reading can answer

The real jurisdiction, the actual users, the budget, the deadlines, the known problems: the repository and the web cannot answer those. These **Human-only gaps** go back grouped, with your best guesses as defaults. With no channel to ask through, they are written as `UNKNOWN` with their uncertainties, listed neatly in the report.

## What you hand back

Summary-first, like every other phase: the `opendomain gate context` verdict in one line, then up to three blockers with their identifiers, then what was filled in (sections, keys, records created or kept), then the sources line by line (identifier, origin, epistemic value), then the Human-only gaps with what would close each one. `opendomain link --check` and the full gate ratify it in an appendix.

The role body keeps the full contract. If this file and the role ever disagree, correct both in the same change — a doctrine that diverges from itself is two doctrines, and one of them is wrong.

# Human-Readable Chat

## Purpose

Make every user-facing chat response clear, natural, concise, and easy to understand.

This skill governs **communication in the chat only**. It does not govern source code, comments in source files, documentation files, commit messages, generated reports, terminal output, or machine-readable artifacts unless the user explicitly asks for those to be written in a human-readable style.

## Core principles

### 1. Talk to the user, not to the terminal

Explain what matters in natural language.

Prefer:

- "J'ai identifié le problème : la validation est effectuée après l'exécution, alors qu'elle devrait la bloquer avant."
- "Le correctif est appliqué. Je vérifie maintenant qu'il ne casse rien."

Avoid:

- "Analysis complete. Root cause identified. Proceeding to remediation."
- "Successfully executed workflow node 4. Status: PASS."

Do not narrate every internal action. Communicate meaningful progress, findings, decisions, and outcomes.

### 2. Use plain language before technical terminology

Start with the meaning or consequence, then introduce the technical term when it helps.

Prefer:
"Deux agents peuvent modifier le même fichier en même temps. Cela crée un risque de conflit."

Instead of:
"Il existe une condition de concurrence sur les écritures concurrentes."

Keep necessary technical terms, identifiers, file paths, error messages, and API names exact. Explain unfamiliar terms briefly rather than replacing them with inaccurate simplifications.

### 3. Structure responses for scanning

Use this default structure when appropriate:

**What matters:** the main conclusion in one or two sentences.

**Why:** the reason or consequence.

**What was done / what comes next:** the action taken, remaining work, or next verification.

Use short paragraphs, descriptive headings, and lists only when they improve comprehension. Do not force every response into a template.

### 4. Be concise without hiding important details

- Lead with the answer, not a long introduction.
- Prefer short sentences and one main idea per paragraph.
- Use bullets for distinct items, not for every sentence.
- Use tables only when comparing multiple options or presenting genuinely tabular information.
- Avoid repeating the user's request before answering it.
- Avoid excessive headings, nested lists, decorative formatting, and unnecessary summaries.
- Expand when the user requests a detailed explanation, audit, tutorial, or complete report.

### 5. Explain code changes through their impact

When reporting implementation work, explain:

- What changed.
- What problem it solves.
- What was verified.
- What remains incomplete or uncertain.

Mention file paths or function names when they help the user locate a change, but explain their significance in ordinary language.

Do not dump large code blocks, diffs, stack traces, or raw command output into the chat unless the user asks for them or they are necessary to diagnose a problem. Extract the relevant evidence and explain it; offer the exact output when useful.

### 6. Distinguish facts, hypotheses, and recommendations

Be explicit about uncertainty.

Use formulations such as:

- "Le test confirme que..."
- "L'erreur semble provenir de..."
- "Une cause possible est..."
- "Je recommande cette approche parce que..."
- "Je n'ai pas encore vérifié ce point."

Never present an assumption as a verified fact. If evidence is missing, say so.

### 7. Report progress honestly

Never claim that a task is complete merely because code was generated, a command was launched, or an agent returned a success message.

Distinguish clearly between:

- **Implemented:** the changes were made.
- **Tested:** the relevant tests or checks were executed.
- **Verified:** the required acceptance criteria were checked and passed.
- **Incomplete:** work or verification remains.

If a command fails, a test is skipped, or a requirement is unmet, explain the consequence and the next step. Do not conceal failures behind positive wording.

### 8. Adapt to the user's level and intent

- For a simple question, answer directly.
- For a complex technical question, explain the key idea first, then the details.
- For debugging, state the likely cause, the evidence, and the next diagnostic or fix.
- For architecture discussions, explain the trade-offs and why a choice matters.
- For implementation tasks, summarize meaningful changes and verification results.
- For educational requests, teach the reasoning instead of merely giving the conclusion.

Do not assume the user is unfamiliar with programming. The objective is clarity, not oversimplification.

### 9. Match the user's language

Respond in the language the user uses, unless they request another language or the context clearly requires it.

For French responses, use natural, professional French. Avoid unnecessary English expressions when a clear French equivalent exists. Preserve English technical names when they are established identifiers.

### 10. Keep the chat free of artificial enthusiasm

Avoid generic openings such as:

- "Great question!"
- "Absolutely!"
- "Excellent work!"
- "I'd be happy to help!"

Avoid congratulatory language, sales-like phrasing, and repetitive reassurance. Start with useful information.

### 11. Make recommendations actionable

When suggesting a next step, explain briefly why it is useful. Do not append a generic "What would you like to do next?" to every answer.

Ask a question only when a missing detail materially affects the result. Otherwise, proceed using reasonable assumptions and state them when necessary.

## Formatting rules

- Use Markdown for readability, not decoration.
- Use **bold** sparingly for important conclusions or statuses.
- Use inline code for identifiers, commands, paths, and technical values.
- Use fenced code blocks only when the code itself is useful.
- Avoid emojis unless the user uses them or they improve the meaning.
- Do not use a status badge for every step.
- Do not repeat the same information in prose, a table, and a summary.

## Non-interference rules

This skill must not:

- Change source-code formatting or implementation choices.
- Modify agent instructions, tools, permissions, or execution plans.
- Reduce tests, verification, security checks, or acceptance criteria.
- Suppress warnings, errors, limitations, or uncertainty.
- Invent completed work or successful test results.
- Replace detailed technical output when the user explicitly requests it.
- Force a specific response template on every message.

## Final principle

**Make the important information easy to understand without making the underlying work less rigorous.**

# Writing a record people and machines can trust

Each registry is a Markdown file made of `##` headings — one per record. The fenced `toml` block is load-bearing and machine-checked (a malformed block is reported with a line number, never guessed at). The prose underneath is never parsed, so write as much explanation as the subject deserves without fear of breaking anything.

````markdown
## REQ-012 — Consult the movement history of an item

```toml
type = "FUNCTIONAL"
status = "DRAFT"
epistemic = "INFERRED"
confidence = "MEDIUM"
actor = ["ACT-002"]
derived-from = ["EVD-014"]
```

**Statement**

The system SHALL allow authorized users to consult the chronological movements
of an item.
````

## Six habits for clean records

1. **Headings follow the pattern exactly**: `## <PREFIX>-<NNN> — Title`. Ask `opendomain new <KIND>` for the next free number (with `--scope` for scoped ids like `REQ-INVENTORY-014`) instead of counting by hand — and re-run it right before writing, since it prints but never reserves.
2. **Links are declared by the dependent side**: `REQ-004 derived-from RULE-001`, never the reverse. If you're unsure which prefix a kind uses or which relations exist, `opendomain reference` knows — don't guess.
3. **Statuses move forward along a lifecycle** — `DRAFT → RESEARCHED → SUPPORTED → VALIDATED → APPROVED → IMPLEMENTING → IMPLEMENTED → VERIFIED` — plus a few terminal states. `opendomain advance` walks an artifact forward and refuses to walk it back; a backwards move means editing the file by hand, deliberately.
4. **An empty registry is a normal starting state**, not a reason to stop: when a file holds only its commented example and its Rules section, follow the example.
5. **One concept, one owner.** If two contexts claim the same word (`SalesCustomer` versus `InventoryCustomer`), merge them or record the distinction as a decision — silent duplication becomes a blocking finding downstream.
6. **Close the loop**: after writing, run `opendomain link --check` and the current gate, then report the verdict with the top blockers quoted by their identifiers.

# Saying how you know

Every record that makes a knowledge claim carries one `epistemic` label. There is no default: a record that makes a claim without saying how it is known is itself a blocking finding (`gate-1/undeclared-epistemic`). The framework cannot protect what it cannot see — so the very first duty is to label honestly.

## The seven states, and when to use each

- **`EXPLICIT`** — a source you actually read states this directly. You record where it came from (`derived-from`). This is the strongest label, and the only one that can carry a `VALIDATED` record.
- **`TACIT`** — real knowledge held in people's practice, written nowhere. Name the practice or the practitioner. It is not "weaker" than `EXPLICIT`, just located differently: what people actually do often matters more than what the document says they do. Record both, and mark the divergence instead of quietly resolving it.
- **`HYBRID`** — part stated in a source, part lived practice. Record both halves and the reasoning that joins them.
- **`INFERRED`** — you derived it by reasoning from evidence. Write down the chain and set a `confidence`. Code you observed in a repository is `INFERRED` at best — never `EXPLICIT`.
- **`ASSUMED`** — nobody knows yet, and you need a placeholder to move forward. Say so in the prose, with the condition that would retire it. User speech, general knowledge, and "typical in this industry" are all `ASSUMED`.
- **`UNKNOWN`** — a known gap. Track it as an uncertainty; do not fill it in with a plausible invention.
- **`CONFLICTING`** — reliable sources disagree. Record both positions and resolve nothing yourself.

## How a claim gets stronger — and how to record it

When a record's status moves to `VALIDATED` or `VERIFIED`, the move itself gets recorded:

```toml
promotions = [
  { from = "ASSUMED", to = "VALIDATED", evidence = ["EVD-014"], date = "2026-04-10" }
]
```

Without that entry, a genuine strengthening and a quiet status edit look identical — and telling them apart is precisely what the framework exists for. A promotion from `ASSUMED` or `INFERRED` to `VALIDATED`/`VERIFIED` that cites no evidence, cites an identifier that doesn't exist, or cites evidence that isn't itself `EXPLICIT` is blocked as `gate-7/epistemic-laundering`. Note there are two tripwires: the recorded history, and the current state alone — a record that reads `ASSUMED` and `VALIDATED` at the same time has been laundered whether or not anyone wrote it down. A workspace with no promotion history at all gets an advisory instead (`gate-7/no-transition-history`): absence of history doesn't prove laundering happened, it proves laundering would currently be undetectable — a smaller problem, and a different one.

## The two things to never do

Never write `EXPLICIT` for something you inferred, and never invent a `SRC-` or `EVD-` identifier to make a claim look sourced. Both turn an honest gap — which the gates know how to handle — into apparent fact, which they cannot.

# Reading a gate result — and acting on it

`opendomain` reads your records and checks the links; it never rewrites them (except through the few commands that say so). Every gate is a pure function: the same workspace always gives the same answer. A blocking finding fails the command with a non-zero exit — which is what makes gates usable as CI steps — while an advisory is reported without failing. Learn both by heart: neither is negotiable at the call site.

## Answer summary-first, never wall-of-text

A raw gate dump is noise; a good report is signal. Always render in this order:

1. **Verdict** — one line: `PASS`, or `FAIL` with the counts (`N blocking, M advisory`).
2. **Top blockers** — at most three, each with the stable identifier the tool printed (like `gate-3/unjustified-requirement`) plus one sentence in your own words. Keep the identifiers verbatim — they are how findings get cited later.
3. **Next action** — exactly one smallest step: the file to open, the source to read, the link to record.
4. **Appendix** — the tool's full output, unedited, for the record.

And three refusals that are not optional: never soften a `FAIL` into "mostly ready"; never describe a blocking finding as advisory because the work feels complete; never edit a record just to silence a finding — that edit is the laundering the framework detects, performed by you. When a gate fails, say it fails, then fix the cause.

## From identifier to action

| What the tool says | What you do |
|---|---|
| `gate-0/no-domain-map`, `gate-0/no-stakeholders` | Complete the context (`/opendomain-project`) |
| `gate-1/no-sources`, `gate-1/orphan-evidence`, `gate-1/undeclared-epistemic` | Research the missing finding (`/opendomain-research`) |
| `gate-1/single-source` | Find a second *independent* source — not a third record on the same one |
| `gate-2/empty-registry`, `gate-2/duplicate-term` | Model the missing piece or merge the duplicates (`/opendomain-domain`) |
| `gate-3/unjustified-requirement`, `gate-3/unresolved-provenance` | Trace to evidence or mark assumed with a tracked uncertainty |
| `gate-5/untraced-specification`, `gate-5/how-not-what` | Derive from the requirement; move the HOW to the plan |
| `gate-6/untraced-task`, `gate-6/dependency-cycle` | Trace the tasks; break the cycle |
| `gate-7/epistemic-laundering`, `gate-7/orphan-test` | Bring explicit evidence or record the promotion honestly; link a test |
| `gate-8/dangling-reference`, `gate-8/assumption-reached-production` | Check the links; resolve the assumption or track it as a risk |

Two syntax notes that save real time: `opendomain gate --through N` takes the gate *number* (0–8), never its name. And `opendomain reference` lists every rule — read it before writing, not after tripping.

# Driving the harness (execution doctrine)

You drive, you do not code around the harness: the `opendomain` CLI implements
this doctrine itself. Your output is a verified agent system, then an archived
run — never an unverified claim.

The loop this doctrine drives is the harness loop, mapped onto the phases
below: plan → identify needs → build each agent and subagent → decide models
per task → tool up (install, verify) → execute by delegation → improve,
amend, iterate.

## The substrate — no new runtime

Nothing below adds a runtime: every capability assembles from OpenCode
primitives, which all reload from disk on save (`/reload` forces a full
reload). The reference frame, translated once and only once:

| What the factory needs | The primitive that provides it |
|---|---|
| Agents + orchestration | `.opencode/agent/<id>.md` files, `mode: primary\|subagent`; a parent admits children through its `subagent` permission — an allowlist of child ids, so a recipe without the entry delegates to nobody (delegation depth ≤ 2, enforced by omission) |
| Per-task model choice | the agent frontmatter `model: provider/model#variant` — the pin the plan report cites, per command override allowed |
| Install & swap tools/skills | skills `.opencode/skills/<id>/SKILL.md` (+ scripts), commands `.opencode/command/<id>.md`, MCP servers `mcp.servers` (local `command[]` / remote url) |
| Sandbox & session layer | ordered permissions `{action, resource, effect}` — the LAST matching rule wins; the shell scanner splits compound commands, so one allow per simple command is the safe recipe (deny first, allows after) |
| Self-improvement | the flow itself rewrites `build`'s node-agents and the registries via `propose`/`apply`/`repatch`; definitions picked up on save — no restart mid-run |

The table is the frame, not the authority: OpenCode V2 evolves, and the
installed version decides. When opencode itself misbehaves — a permission
that did not bite, an MCP server that will not start, a definition that did
not reload — go in this order: the installed binary first (`opencode
--help`, `--version`, `opencode mcp list`, `opencode auth list`), then the
doc index at <https://opencode.ai/v2/llms.txt> (agents, skills, commands,
permissions, MCP servers, config, troubleshooting — one page per question),
then the `opencode` skill when the project or user installs it. Never retype
what the help already answers; when the table and the installed opencode
disagree, the binary wins and a lesson records which line drifted.

## Phase 1 — Construction (before any business code)

1. **Task `T`** — it lives in the registries. `opendomain plan TASK-012`
   resolves the task record as `T` (title, objective/constraints/criteria
   prose, `derived-from SPEC/RULE` links) and compiles the DAG from it. For
   work outside the registries, `opendomain spec new <slug>` writes
   `opendomain/harness/specs/<slug>/spec.md` — objective, constraints
   (`interdiction de X` lines), acceptance criteria.
2. **Grounding**: `opendomain ground <slug>` collects repo, manifests and
   toolchain into `grounding/<slug>/repo-scan.md` + fingerprint. Manual notes
   go in the same folder.
3. **DAG**: `opendomain plan <slug>` compiles via opencode (the real
   decomposition, verified by the loop); `opendomain plan <slug> --offline`
   asks the deterministic fallback explicitly (CI, no network). Incomplete
   agents are refused at admission.
4. **Execution kit**: `opendomain build <slug>` equips every agent in
   `agents/<slug>/` — `AGENTS.md` (the shared contract: loop, tools, context
   & memory, sandbox, hooks, skills), `<id>.md` (σ_i: role, tool whitelist,
   I/O contract, criteria), `<id>.kit.json` (machine manifest) —
   **resolves every node's kit** against the component registry (`kit`:
   skills, commands, protocols — a capacity without a provider is a typed
   construction fault; `--fetch` admits explicit web-provisioning with
   provenance), and **defines the node-agents** in `.opencode/agent/`: one
   file per node, deny-universal first, one allow per whitelisted tool, the
   output contract and the resolved kit in the body. Visible and reviewable
   BEFORE the run; the run invokes them, it never rewrites them. Targeted
   fixes only; `opendomain validate` replays the static graph checks.

## Phase 2 — Execution under gates

5. `opendomain run <slug>` — the executor is opencode, the real, visible,
   archived path (mock stays the offline self-check via `opendomain bench`);
   agents run in topological order; the coordinator applies the gate
   `y_i ∈ C_i` (schema, patterns, test commands executed in the sandbox)
   **before** any propagation; attempts replay with typed feedback, bounded
   by `[gates] max_attempts` in `opendomain.toml`.
6. The run archives append-only under `runs/run-NNN-<slug>/`:
   `trace.jsonl` (Start/Passed/Retry/Failed), `context/` (the `y_i`),
   `gates.log`, the frozen graph. Nothing is lost; everything replays.
7. **Terminal failure → attribution**: `opendomain attribute <run>` types it —
   `criteria_failure` / `spec_mismatch` → **local**: fix, then
   `opendomain run <slug> --resume <run>`; `grounding_failure` →
   **upstream**: re-ground, re-plan that node alone; `contract_violation` →
   **structural**: re-plan the sub-graph (`opendomain repatch <run>`), a
   partial return to phase 1.
8. **A posteriori control**: `opendomain verify <run>` replays every gate on
   the archived outputs — at any time, without an LLM.

## Prohibitions

- propagate unverified output (no exception — `gates.strict = true`);
- invent a tool outside an agent's whitelist (least privilege is projected
  into the executor: deny first, one allow per tool);
- run a command outside the sandbox while `[sandbox] enabled = true`;
- produce final code with no **verifier** node in the graph;
- blind retry without typed feedback (each attempt is directed by the gate);
- re-plan the whole system for a local error — recovery cost follows the
  locality of the error.

# From keywords to evidence you can build on

Good research ends in saturation and corroboration — not in a pile of notes from a single source. The path has three stages: fan out widely, record richly, triangulate and stop.

## 1. Fan out from keywords, in parallel

Start from 5–12 keywords drawn from `project.md`, the `[project]` table, and the question at hand — domain nouns, the jurisdiction, the stack, any regulation glimpsed in code or docs. Turn them into 3–6 search directions and work each one in parallel: the regulation or standard, the vendor's official documentation, industry practice, competitors (as clues only — a competitor page is evidence, never a justification), and textbooks or academic references. Give each thread one sharp question plus its keyword cluster, and keep threads independent: they never share citations.

Trust has an order: a regulation or standard outranks official docs, which outrank textbooks, which outrank heard practice, which outranks competitor marketing. Note web sources with their URL and retrieval date, repo files with path and revision — and never cite a file you haven't opened yourself.

## 2. Record each source richly

Every accepted source becomes a `SRC-` record (`opendomain new SRC`): title, type, address, today's date as `retrieved`, and the exact sections you used. Then each finding becomes its own `EVD-` record (`opendomain new EVD`): a `type` from the vocabulary (`USER_NEED`, `DOMAIN_FACT`, `BUSINESS_RULE`, `INDUSTRY_PRACTICE`, `REGULATORY_REQUIREMENT`, `TECHNICAL_CONSTRAINT`, `COMPETITOR_CAPABILITY`, `MARKET_SIGNAL`, `ASSUMPTION`, `HYPOTHESIS`, `INFERENCE`), a `Statement` phrased in the source's own terms, an `Exact context` (section, page, revision), a `Not claimed` section saying what the source does *not* establish, a `derived-from` link to the source, and an honest epistemic value with its confidence.

## 3. Triangulate, then stop

Corroboration means two or more *independent* sources saying the same thing. Three records resting on one source is restatement, not corroboration — the gates block it as `gate-1/single-source`. When sources disagree, open a conflict record with both positions and leave the resolution pending; resolve nothing yourself. A gap becomes a tracked uncertainty. An unreadable source goes under retrieval failures and is never cited.

Stop a direction when new sources only restate what you already have — that's saturation. Report each direction as saturated or still thin, and name the exact source that would close the thin ones. Research ends at findings; turning them into requirements is a later step, with its own discipline.

# Working under OpenDomain

Welcome. This project keeps what it knows about its domain in `opendomain/` — small linked records written in Markdown — and the `opendomain` command checks that the links hold. Think of `opendomain` as the project's memory: whenever you wonder whether something here is known, inferred, or merely assumed, ask `opendomain` instead of guessing.

`opendomain` reads that knowledge. It never rewrites your records, except through the few commands that say so explicitly (`init`, `link`, `advance`, `propose`, `apply`, `archive`).

## Where to look, depending on your task

This file states the one discipline everyone shares. The operative know-how lives in six focused skills — load the one your task needs:

| When you need to... | Load this skill |
|---|---|
| Choose an `epistemic` value, record a promotion, check for laundering | `.opencode/skills/opendomain-epistemics/SKILL.md` |
| Write or repair any artifact — format, ids, relations | `.opencode/skills/opendomain-artifacts/SKILL.md` |
| Gather external evidence — parallel search, triangulation | `.opencode/skills/opendomain-research/SKILL.md` |
| Read a gate, status, or audit output — and fix what it reports | `.opencode/skills/opendomain-gates/SKILL.md` |
| Execute work by agents — build the agent system from a `TASK-###`, then drive the run under gates and recover it | `.opencode/skills/opendomain-harness/SKILL.md` |
| Complete or refresh project context — Phase 0: `project.md`, `[project]`, first `DOM`/`STK` | `.opencode/skills/context-completer/SKILL.md` |

## The one discipline everyone shares

Every record that makes a knowledge claim carries an `epistemic` label saying how the claim is known: `EXPLICIT` (a source you read says so) · `TACIT` (lived practice, unwritten) · `HYBRID` (a bit of both) · `INFERRED` (you derived it — show the chain) · `ASSUMED` (nobody knows yet — say so) · `UNKNOWN` (a known gap — track it, don't fill it) · `CONFLICTING` (sources disagree — record both, resolve nothing).

Two things are never acceptable. Writing `EXPLICIT` for something you inferred is called epistemic laundering — presenting an invented domain rule as established fact — and it is the exact failure this whole framework exists to catch. A confident rule built on general knowledge, with no source behind it, is `ASSUMED` with the reasoning written down. And never invent a `SRC-` or `EVD-` identifier to make a claim look sourced: a fabricated citation is worse than an honest gap, because it flows downstream through every gate and becomes indistinguishable from a real one.

## Which `opendomain` command answers your question

| Your question | The command |
|---|---|
| Where does the project stand? | `opendomain status` |
| Why does this artifact exist? | `opendomain trace <ID>` |
| What implements and verifies it? | `opendomain trace <ID> --forward` |
| Who said so, nearest source first? | `opendomain trace <ID> --provenance` |
| What breaks if this changes? | `opendomain impact <ID>` |
| What does the graph look like? | `opendomain graph [--root <ID>] [--depth N] [--dot]` |
| Is it consistent enough to proceed? | `opendomain gate <gate>` |
| Is anything dangling or unjustified? | `opendomain audit`, `opendomain link --check` |
| What do the identifiers mean? | `opendomain reference` |
| Record a link / next free id / move along the lifecycle | `opendomain link`, `opendomain new`, `opendomain advance` |

The gates are named `context`, `research`, `domain`, `requirements`, `opportunity`, `specification`, `plan`, `implementation`, `completion`. If a command you expected does not exist, `opendomain --help` is authoritative — don't assume a convenient command into existence.

## When you report

A failing gate carries a stable identifier, like `gate-3/unjustified-requirement`. Quote it as-is. Never describe a blocking finding as advisory because the surrounding work looks finished, and never edit a record just to silence a finding — that edit is the laundering, performed by you. When a gate fails, say it fails, then fix the cause.

# OpenDomain

**Domain-first, evidence-driven engineering for AI coding assistants.**
From real-world knowledge to validated software — with every claim traced, graded, gated, and executed by agents that cannot propagate unverified output.

[Documentation](https://gayensis09.github.io/OpenDomain/) · [Spécification](https://gayensis09.github.io/OpenDomain/docs/theory.html) · [MIT](https://github.com/GAYENSIS09/OpenDomain/blob/HEAD/LICENSE)

[![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/opendomain-cli.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/opendomain-cli)
[![docs.rs](https://img.shields.io/docsrs/opendomain-cli.svg)](https://docs.rs/opendomain-cli)
![Rust 1.75+](https://img.shields.io/badge/rust-1.75%2B-orange)
![154 tests passing](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-154_passing-green)
![9 deterministic gates](https://img.shields.io/badge/gates-9_deterministic-blue)
![37 artifact kinds](https://img.shields.io/badge/artifacts-37_kinds-red)
![MIT license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-lightgrey)

> **The failure OpenDomain catches:** an AI coding assistant produces syntactically complete, internally consistent, test-passing software whose **domain semantics were invented rather than known**. That is not a modelling error — it is an *epistemic* one. The assistant cannot distinguish a reconstructed domain rule from a plausible hallucination, because nothing records what is known, assumed, inferred, or unknown.
>
> **OpenDomain stores that distinction explicitly and enforces it mechanically** — twice over: at rest, on the linked artifacts of the workspace; at runtime, on every output an execution agent produces before that output reaches its consumers.

## What it gives you

| Capability | How |
|---|---|
| **Epistemic honesty** | Every artifact carries `EXPLICIT` · `TACIT` · `HYBRID` · `INFERRED` · `ASSUMED` · `UNKNOWN` · `CONFLICTING` |
| **Traceability spine** | One ordered chain: source → evidence → domain → requirement → spec → plan → code → test → validation |
| **Two mechanical answers** | `opendomain trace REQ-012` — *why does this exist?* · `opendomain impact RULE-007` — *what breaks if this changes?* |
| **9 deterministic gates** | 63 named rules (`gate-3/unjustified-requirement`, …). Pure functions: no mutation, stable slugs, exact citations |
| **Verified execution** | A DAG of agents runs under the same discipline: every output passes its rejection gate (`yᵢ ∈ Cᵢ`) before it propagates — *Generate → Verify → Attribute → Refine* |
| **Agent-native** | `AGENTS.md`, 15 slash-commands, 3 role agents, 7 skills - generated by `opendomain init` for any coding agent |

> The agent-executed flow, end to end — the six phases, the run archive, the typed attributions — is documented in [The harness](https://gayensis09.github.io/OpenDomain/docs/harness.html).

```bash
opendomain trace REQ-012          # why does this exist?
opendomain impact RULE-007        # if this changes, what breaks?
```

## Install

Requires **Rust 1.75+**. No clone needed — `cargo install` puts `opendomain` in `~/.cargo/bin`, already on your `PATH`:

```bash
cargo install opendomain-cli                                            # from crates.io
cargo install --git https://github.com/GAYENSIS09/OpenDomain --locked opendomain-cli   # from this repository
opendomain --version
```

Alternative from a checkout:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/GAYENSIS09/OpenDomain
cd OpenDomain
cargo install --path crates/opendomain-cli --locked
```

## Start here

```bash
mkdir my-project && cd my-project
opendomain init --name my-project
opendomain status
```

`opendomain init` **installs only** — registries + `opendomain.toml` + the agent contract. It records no context: run `/opendomain-project` afterwards to fill `project.md`, `[project]`, `DOM-001`/`STK-001` from the repository, external research, then user answers. Each generated tree carries its own `.gitignore` — regenerable like the rest of the scaffold, and the project's own `.gitignore` is never touched: a project that versions a tree (the registries are the cited F14/L9 evidence) deletes that tree's `.gitignore`. Inside a git repository it advises the split (the registries are the cited evidence, `opendomain provenance` verifies the citations).

Beyond the `opendomain/` directory of **42 files** — 34 registry files (one per artifact kind, from `SRC` to `TEST`), six explanatory files (`README.md`, `project.md`, the research protocol, the architecture overview, the specs and changes READMEs), `opendomain.toml` and the tree's own `.gitignore` — it writes the **agent contract** at the project root, so the framework is usable by any coding agent rather than only by someone who has read the paper: `AGENTS.md` plus the `.opencode/` tree (15 commands, 3 role agents, 7 skills, and the tree's own `.gitignore`). **In total, `opendomain init` writes 69 files.** It is idempotent — re-running it reports what already exists and changes nothing.

```
AGENTS.md                          # the rules, readable by any agent
.opencode/command/                 # /opendomain-status, /opendomain-gate, /opendomain-trace, /opendomain-impact,
                                   # /opendomain-audit, /opendomain-record, /opendomain-project, /opendomain-research,
                                   # /opendomain-domain, /opendomain-requirements, /opendomain-opportunity,
                                   # /opendomain-spec, /opendomain-plan, /opendomain-harness, /opendomain-complete
.opencode/agent/                   # context-completer, domain-researcher, opendomain-harness
.opencode/skills/                  # opendomain, -artifacts, -epistemics, -research, -gates, -harness, context-completer
```

`AGENTS.md` is never overwritten, not even with `--force`: if you already keep your own, `opendomain` does not claim it. The namespaced `.opencode/` files are written by `opendomain` and are refreshed by `--force`.

```bash
opendomain init --profile lean # start at Stage 3; the domain model exists elsewhere
opendomain init --profile core # stages 0, 1, 3-8 (no opportunity discovery)
opendomain init --profile full # everything (default)
opendomain init --dry-run # report what would happen, write nothing
```

> **New to OpenDomain?** Start with the [documentation](https://gayensis09.github.io/OpenDomain/) — [5-minute guide](https://gayensis09.github.io/OpenDomain/docs/getting-started.html) → [core concepts](https://gayensis09.github.io/OpenDomain/docs/concepts.html) → [the 9 gates](https://gayensis09.github.io/OpenDomain/docs/gates.html).

## Working with `opendomain`

`opendomain` **reads and checks**; it does not author. You write the artifacts, `opendomain` tells you whether they are consistent.

```bash
opendomain status                        # where does the project actually stand?
opendomain gate context                  # what is missing before the domain can start?
opendomain gate --through 2               # run every gate up to the domain stage (0-8)

opendomain link --check                  # every referenced id must exist
opendomain link REQ-012 derived-from EVD-014   # declare an edge (writes the TOML block)
opendomain advance REQ-012 VALIDATED     # move along the lifecycle
opendomain show REQ-012                  # one artifact's full record

opendomain trace REQ-012                 # why does this exist?
opendomain trace --forward REQ-012       # what implements and verifies it?
opendomain impact RULE-007               # what breaks if this changes?
opendomain graph --root REQ-012 --depth 3
opendomain audit                         # traceability health across the workspace
opendomain reference                     # the gates and the 37 artifact kinds
opendomain export                        # the whole base as one paginated PDF (Mermaid graph inside)
```

The verification subsystem (Sections 9/10 of the paper — the rigour table, the
generated executable specifications, the binding-provenance record, the
provisioner, in that order, each gated on the previous):

```bash
opendomain rigour                        # the §9.7 rigour table + workspace audit
opendomain provision --dry-run           # stack detection + ordered selection, nothing written
opendomain provision                     # generated .feature scaffolds (@AC tags, provenance) — or a recorded refusal
opendomain bind                          # binding provenance + verification depth audit (findings, not gate rules)
opendomain provenance                    # verifies each run citation against the archived run it names (F14)
```

Change proposals follow the OpenSpec layout:

```bash
opendomain propose tighten-reservation --summary "Tighten the reservation window"
opendomain apply tighten-reservation
opendomain archive tighten-reservation
```

### The nine gates

```
0         1          2        3              4             5               6      7                8
context → research → domain → requirements → opportunity → specification → plan → implementation → completion
```

Cumulative: passing gate 8 means gates 0–7 passed too.

| Gate | Question it asks |
| ---- | ---------------- |
| `context` | Do we know what we are building, and what is already true? |
| `research` | Is the domain understood well enough to derive requirements? |
| `domain` | Is the domain model coherent, owned and cross-linked? |
| `requirements` | Is every requirement justified, testable and traced? |
| `opportunity` | Has anything been challenged, and is the chosen concept earned? |
| `specification` | Does the specification describe observable behaviour and nothing else? |
| `plan` | Is there a bounded, ordered plan that can realise the specification? |
| `implementation` | Did implementation satisfy the acceptance criteria without drift? |
| `completion` | Is the whole chain coherent, tested and free of critical unknowns? |

`opendomain reference` prints this list as a rendered report; `opendomain reference --json` returns it machine-readably, grouped by gate, with each rule's severity.

Findings carry one of two severities. `Blocking` fails the command — `opendomain` exits non-zero — and means the phase cannot be considered complete. `Advisory` is reported and does not fail the command. The paper specifies three levels (`BLOCKER`, `WARNING`, `NOTE`); the implementation has two, and the paper's Section 11.7 records the six conditions whose severity disagrees with its own specification.

Gates are pure functions from the workspace to a report: they never mutate state, so running one twice gives the same answer, and a failure names the exact condition that broke.

### Scripts and CI

`--json` works on every command that reports. A failing gate exits non-zero, so `opendomain gate --through 5` works as a CI step.

```bash
opendomain gate --through 5 --json > gate-report.json
```

`--no-color` and `-C <dir>` are available everywhere. `--strict` is accepted for explicitness and currently changes nothing: blocking findings always fail the command and advisory ones never do. `advisory_gates` in `opendomain.toml` and the `[schemas]` section are likewise written by `opendomain init` but not read by the CLI today.

## Using it with opencode

This repository ships a working opencode integration. If you point opencode at a project that has an `opendomain/` workspace, the following become available automatically.

**Slash commands**

| Command | What it does |
| ------- | ------------ |
| `/opendomain-status` | Where the project stands, and what is blocking |
| `/opendomain-gate <gate>` | Runs a gate and reports the findings verbatim |
| `/opendomain-trace <ID>` | Explains why an artifact exists, from its recorded links |
| `/opendomain-impact <ID>` | What a change to an artifact would break |
| `/opendomain-audit` | Traceability health before claiming work is done |
| `/opendomain-record <topic>` | Writes a domain artifact, keeping its epistemic state honest |
| `/opendomain-project` | Completes Phase 0 context (repo scan + external research + user questions) |
| `/opendomain-research` | Gate 1 research, parallel keyword fan-out via `domain-researcher` |
| `/opendomain-domain` | Gate 2 domain model increment |
| `/opendomain-requirements` | Gate 3 justified, testable requirements |
| `/opendomain-opportunity` | Gate 4 challenged concept + falsifiable hypothesis |

| `/opendomain-plan` | Gate 6 bounded, ordered plan |

One command per gate keeps usage simple: run the command for the stage you are in; it loads the skill, delegates to the right subagent, then shows `opendomain gate` verbatim. No extra orchestration to learn.

**Subagents** (only 3 — one role each, calling each other)

- `context-completer` — owns Phase 0 (`project.md` + `[project]` + `DOM-001`/`STK-001`). Reads the repo itself, **delegates external research to `domain-researcher`**, then asks human-only gaps. Called by `/opendomain-project`.
- `domain-researcher` — evidence specialist. Called by `context-completer`, `/opendomain-research`, `/opendomain-domain`, `/opendomain-requirements`; fans out 3-6 axes in parallel itself. Bash `deny` by default with `opendomain *` + read-only repo commands allowed.
- `opendomain-harness` — execution architect: one `TASK-###` record becomes a planned, grounded, gated, archived agent system; failures come back typed (`local`/`upstream`/`structural`). Doctrine in the skill `opendomain-harness`; called by `/opendomain-harness`, the only door into agent-executed work.

**Skills** (the framework's strength, loaded on demand by commands and agents)

| Skill | Loads when |
|---|---|
| `opendomain` (index) | Always-available summary; points to the five below |
| `opendomain-epistemics` | Choosing a value, recording a promotion, checking laundering |

**Skill.** `.opencode/skills/opendomain/SKILL.md` loads on demand and carries the artifact format and the epistemic discipline. `AGENTS.md` holds the short version that is always in context, so the skill does not have to be.

```json
{
 "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
 "permission": {
 "bash": {
 "opendomain *": "allow",
 "opendomain init *": "ask",

 "opendomain archive *": "ask"

}
```

`opendomain *` is allowed and the five mutating subcommands are asked for, so reading the project is frictionless and changing it still needs consent. The `domain-researcher` subagent is stricter still: its own frontmatter denies all bash except `opendomain *`, so it can check its work and can run nothing else.

## The artifact format

Each registry is a Markdown file of `##` headings, one per artifact. A fenced `toml` block carries the machine-checked fields; the prose below is for humans and is never parsed.

````markdown
## REQ-012 — Consult the movement history of an item

```toml
type = "FUNCTIONAL"
status = "DRAFT"
epistemic = "INFERRED"
confidence = "MEDIUM"
actor = ["ACT-002"]
derived-from = ["EVD-014"]
rules = ["RULE-007"]
```

**Statement**

The system SHALL allow authorized users to consult the chronological movements
of an item.
````

A malformed TOML block is reported with a line number, never guessed at. The prose is free-form, so you can write as much explanation as the subject deserves without risking a parse error.

Identifiers carry their kind as a prefix — `REQ`, `EVD`, `SRC`, `RULE`, `AC`, `SPEC` and 31 others (`opendomain reference` lists them all) — optionally scoped, as in `REQ-INVENTORY-014` and `AC-INVENTORY-014-01`. Links are declared by the artifact that depends on the other, not the reverse: `REQ-004 derived-from RULE-001`.

## What gets enforced

The nine gates carry 63 named rules, each identified by a stable slug such as `gate-3/unjustified-requirement` so a failure can be cited rather than paraphrased. A representative selection:

| Rule | What it forbids |
| ---- | --------------- |
| `gate-3/unjustified-requirement` | A requirement with no `derived-from` an evidence record or business rule |
| `gate-1/orphan-evidence` | An evidence record not `derived-from` a source. An unsourced claim is not evidence |
| `gate-1/single-source` | Every evidence record citing the same single source — a claim repeated by one origin is not corroborated |
| `gate-8/assumption-reached-production` | A requirement whose `epistemic` is `ASSUMED`, `UNKNOWN` or `CONFLICTING` reaching the specification stage |
| `gate-5/how-not-what` | A specification that states mechanism rather than observable behaviour |
| `gate-4/unfalsifiable-hypothesis` | A hypothesis with no metric and no failure condition |
| `gate-4/feature-cloning` | A concept justified only by competitor parity |
| `gate-6/dependency-cycle` | Task dependencies forming a cycle |
| `gate-8/requirement-without-passing-test` | A requirement marked `IMPLEMENTED` with no verified test downstream |
| `gate-8/dangling-reference` | A link pointing at an identifier that does not exist |
| `gate-1/undeclared-epistemic` | An artifact that makes a claim but declares no epistemic state |
| `gate-7/epistemic-laundering` | An `ASSUMED` or `INFERRED` artifact marked `VALIDATED` or `VERIFIED`, with no intervening `EXPLICIT` evidence |

`opendomain audit` reports traceability health across the whole workspace, including coverage ratios, unjustified artifacts, dangling links, and open conflicts.

## Recording how a claim got stronger

An artifact's `epistemic` state is a claim about the present. A `promotions` array records how it got there:

````markdown
```toml
status = "VALIDATED"
epistemic = "EXPLICIT"
promotions = [
 { from = "ASSUMED", to = "VALIDATED", evidence = ["EVD-014"], date = "2026-04-10" }
]
```
````

Without that record, a change from `ASSUMED` to `EXPLICIT` and a change of status are indistinguishable from each other — which is precisely the edit the framework exists to catch. `gate-7/epistemic-laundering` blocks a promotion from `ASSUMED` or `INFERRED` into `VALIDATED` or `VERIFIED` that cites no evidence, cites evidence that does not exist, or cites evidence that is not itself `EXPLICIT`. It also blocks on the current state alone: an artifact that is `ASSUMED` and `VALIDATED` at once has been laundered whether or not it wrote anything down.

A workspace that records no promotions at all gets an advisory, not a blocking finding. Absence of history is not evidence that laundering happened; it is evidence that laundering is currently undetectable, which is a smaller problem and a different one.

# Changes

In-flight work lives here, one directory per change proposal.

A **change** is a modification to already-agreed behaviour. The registries
record what the project currently believes; a change records a proposal to
alter that, reviewed and then applied or rejected.

## Why changes are separate

Keeping proposals out of the registries is what makes `opendomain status` meaningful. If
`REQ-004` could be edited directly, the registry would always describe an
ambiguous mix of agreed and proposed behaviour, and no gate could tell them
apart.

## Layout

```text
changes/
  add-over-receipt-approval/
    proposal.md      # why, what changes, which IDs are affected
    design.md        # how, for changes large enough to need it
    tasks.md         # the ordered work
    specs/           # capability deltas, same format as specs/
    tests.md         # what will verify it
```

## Lifecycle

```text
PROPOSED -apply-> APPLIED -archive-> ARCHIVED
    |                                      |
    +-reject-> REJECTED                     +- superseded by a later change
```

A change is never edited in place after it is applied. Correcting an applied
change means another change.

## Rules

- Every change names the IDs it affects. A change that cannot say what it
  touches is a rewrite, not a change.
- `proposal.md` must state *why* before *what*. A proposal that leads with
  implementation has already skipped the interesting part.
- Anything that survives application is copied into the registries by
  `opendomain apply`; the change directory is then the historical record of how it
  arrived.
- A rejected change is archived, not deleted. Knowing what was considered and
  why it lost is worth more than a clean directory.

Candidate solutions worth debating, `CPT-###`. One artifact per concept.

A concept is a *shape* of solution, not a task list. Two concepts are worth
writing down when the team disagrees about which is better, because then the
disagreement is a real decision with real consequences.

Required fields: `status`, `class`, `rationale`. Recommended: `mechanism`,
`key-difference`, `derived-from`.

`class` is one of `INCREMENTAL` `REVOLUTIONARY` `REPLICATION` `SUBSTITUTION`.

## Rules for this registry

- A concept with no `mechanism` and no `key-difference` is a slogan. Gate 4
  reports it.
- `class = "REPLICATION"` justified by "our competitor has it" is feature
  cloning. Gate 4 blocks it. Competitor functionality is evidence about a
  market, not a reason to build.
- Write the concept that you expect to lose. A registry where every concept
  wins is a registry where nothing was debated.

**Never arbitrarily select one source without documenting why.** A conflict that
is resolved silently becomes an undocumented assumption, and undocumented
assumptions are what audits find last and most expensively.

`OPEN` — disagreement recorded, no decision taken
`RESOLVED` — a decision was taken and justified below
`CONTEXTUAL` — both are true, in different regimes; both rules are recorded

Boundaries the project does not choose, `CNST-###`. One artifact per constraint.

A constraint narrows the solution space from outside. A decision narrows it
from inside. Recording a decision as a constraint is how a project ends up
pretending it had no choice.

Required fields: `status`, `type`, `statement`. Recommended: `source`,
`derived-from`, `implications`.

`type` is one of `TECHNICAL` `LEGAL` `REGULATORY` `FINANCIAL` `ORGANIZATIONAL` `TEMPORAL` `PHYSICAL` `CONTRACTUAL`.

- Every constraint needs an origin. An unsourced constraint is a preference
  wearing a bureaucratic costume.
- State the consequences, not just the boundary. A constraint whose cost is not
  written down will be dropped under pressure.
- A constraint that is really a decision belongs in `DEC-###` or an `ADR`.

A contract is an agreement about a boundary: an API, an event, a file format, a
database shape that another system reads. If nobody else is affected, it is
internal design, and it belongs in the plan.

Required fields: `status`, `type`, `derived-from`, `version`. Recommended:
`verification`, `consumers`, `breaking-change`.

`type` is one of `API` `EVENT` `DATA` `FILE_FORMAT` `LIBRARY`.

A contradiction is not a source conflict. `XCONF` is two sources disagreeing;
`CON` is the project asserting two incompatible things. The second is almost
always more expensive.

Required fields: `status`, `statement`, `side-a`, `side-b`.

A context is a region of the domain where a particular meaning of a term holds
and one set of rules applies. Modules are not contexts; a module that serves two
contexts is a coupling problem, not a modelling win.

Required fields: `purpose`, `status`.

- Every important concept has exactly one owning context. If two contexts both

- A new module is never an isolated application. Adding one means re-running

# Entities

Domain entities, `ENT-###`. The conceptual model, not the database.

Required fields: `status`, `owned-by`.

For every concept ask:

- Does this exist in the domain, independently of our software?
- What evidence supports it?
- What behaviour or rule requires it?
- Is it actually a separate concept?
- Would it be a value object instead?
- Is it an implementation artefact rather than domain knowledge?

**Do not create a class because a noun appears in a requirement.**

- An entity needs a lifecycle worth modelling only if it has states; if it has

- Shared entities have exactly one owner. Consumers link to it.

This registry is the load-bearing one. A requirement with no evidence upstream

`statement` must be what the source says, in the source's terms. Your reading
of it goes in `interpreted-as`, separately, so the two can be challenged
independently.

## Evidence types

`USER_NEED` `DOMAIN_FACT` `BUSINESS_RULE` `INDUSTRY_PRACTICE`
`REGULATORY_REQUIREMENT` `TECHNICAL_CONSTRAINT` `COMPETITOR_CAPABILITY`
`MARKET_SIGNAL` `ASSUMPTION` `HYPOTHESIS` `INFERENCE`

## Rules for this registry

- **Evidence is not a requirement.** The chain is
  `Source → Finding → Interpretation → Candidate Need → Requirement`. Skipping a
  step is how a competitor feature becomes a requirement.
- A `COMPETITOR_CAPABILITY` is evidence about a market, never a requirement
  for this project.
- Two sources that share an origin are one source. Gate 1 blocks when every
  evidence record cites a single source.
- Record what the evidence does *not* claim. Absence is easy to overlook and
  expensive to discover late.
- `epistemic = "INFERRED"` requires the reasoning to be written out in the
  body. An unexplained inference is an assumption wearing a costume.

## Recording a promotion

When an artifact's `status` advances to `VALIDATED` or `VERIFIED`, record the
move in `promotions`. This is the only way the tool can tell a promotion backed
by new evidence from a status typed by hand.

```toml
status = "VALIDATED"
epistemic = "EXPLICIT"
promotions = [
  { from = "ASSUMED", to = "VALIDATED", evidence = ["EVD-014"], date = "2026-04-10" }
]
```

`from` and `evidence` and `date` are optional to write and not optional to
mean. Gate 7 blocks when a promotion from `ASSUMED` or `INFERRED` into
`VALIDATED` or `VERIFIED` cites no evidence, cites evidence that is missing, or
cites evidence that is not itself `EXPLICIT`. It also blocks on the current
state: an artifact that is `ASSUMED` and `VALIDATED` at the same time is
laundered whether or not it recorded anything.

A promotion citing explicit evidence is how an assumption stops being one. The
record is the difference between having changed your mind and having relabelled
the artifact.

# Hypotheses

Falsifiable claims, `HYP-###`. One artifact per hypothesis.

A hypothesis is not a belief. It is a sentence with a metric and a condition
that would prove it wrong. If you cannot write the failing condition, you have
an opinion, and the opinion belongs in a decision record instead.

Required fields: `status`, `statement`, `metric`, `fails-when`. Gate 4 blocks
any hypothesis missing the last two.

<!--

```toml

derived-from = ["CPT-003", "EVD-021", "OPP-002"]
tested-by = ["EXP-002"]
confidence = "MEDIUM"
```

**Statement**

Replacing manual entry with scan-and-confirm will reduce manual re-keying of
received line items to under 2%, from the 18% measured in `EVD-021`.

**Metric**

Share of received line items requiring manual entry, measured over one week
with at least 200 receipts.

**Failing condition**

- The rate exceeds 8% overall, **or**
- It exceeds 10% for any single supplier

## Rules for this registry

- A hypothesis without a `fails-when` cannot be tested, so it is not a
  hypothesis. Gate 4 blocks it.
- Choose the failing condition **before** the experiment. A threshold chosen
  afterwards is not a threshold.
- A refuted hypothesis is a good outcome. Record it.

# Research protocol

How this project finds out things. Run the stages in order; do not skip to
searching.

## Source hierarchy

Prefer the highest tier that answers the question. The ranking is contextual,
not absolute: a competitor's own workflow documentation often beats a generic
article when you need to understand a concrete process.

1. Laws, regulations, official standards
2. Official institutional documentation
3. Professional bodies and recognised organisations
4. Peer-reviewed research
5. Academic textbooks
6. Official product and process documentation
7. Industry reports and case studies
8. Established professional publications
9. Open-source implementations
10. Competitor documentation
11. Community discussion
12. Blogs and informal content

Ask "authoritative for *what*?" before citing.

## Search stages

- **A — Seed.** Broad, authoritative queries: `"<domain> requirements | workflow"`.
- **B — Concept expansion.** Take the terminology from your strongest sources
  and search *those* terms.
- **C — Backward.** For important academic sources, read the references.
  Foundational models and earlier theories live there.
- **D — Forward.** Find later work that cites your important sources.
- **E — Contradiction.** Search deliberately for disagreement:
  `"<concept> limitations | exceptions | criticism | failure"`.
- **F — Regional.** Search local regulation, terminology and practice:
  `"<domain> <country> | local regulation"`.

Never assume a generic international workflow represents local practice.

Behavioural specifications, `SPEC-###`. One file per capability.

A specification states **what the system does that can be observed**. It does
not state how, and it does not state why — the requirement already did that.

## File layout

```text
specs/
  receipts/
    SPEC-004-receiving-goods.md
  procurement/
    SPEC-002-purchase-orders.md
  overview.md
```

Each file is a registry containing one or more `SPEC-###` artifacts, so the
same parser reads it.

## The five obligatory sections

1. **Scenarios** — Given / When / Then, with the precondition made concrete
2. **Behavioural rules** — SHALL statements, numbered
3. **Acceptance criteria** — `AC-###-##` per scenario, one observable outcome
   each
4. **Edge cases** — what happens at zero, at the boundary, and on conflict
5. **Non-goals** — what this capability deliberately does not do

## Given / When / Then, used properly

The **Given** must make the precondition real: actual values, not placeholders.
The **Then** must be observable from outside: a value, a state, an event, an
absence of an effect.

## Rules for these files

- **What, not how.** Gate 5 reports a specification that names a database, a
  framework or a message broker. The technology belongs in the plan or an ADR.
- Every scenario is executable as a test. If it cannot be, it is prose.
- A criterion is one outcome. "The system works correctly" is not a criterion.
- Write the **Non-goals** section every time. It is the section that stops the
  specification from quietly growing.

# Acceptance tests

Executable verification, `TEST-###`. One artifact per test.

A test is the executable form of an acceptance criterion. If a criterion cannot
be written as a test, the criterion is not finished.

Required fields: `status`, `verifies`, `level`, `assertions`. Recommended:
`automation`, `environment`, `tolerance`.

`level` is one of `UNIT` `INTEGRATION` `CONTRACT` `E2E` `LOAD` `SECURITY`.

`status` uses the normal lifecycle. **`VERIFIED` means the test has been run
and passed against the current implementation** — not that it was written.
Gate 8 checks for this.

### Verification depth and binding provenance

Two optional fields make a test's claim inspectable (Sections 10.9/10.10):

```toml
verification-depth = "executed"   # executed | discovered | declared
binding = { to = "AC-004-03", provisionance = "ANNOTATED", confirmed = false }
```

- `verification-depth` — `executed`: the suite was run against the current
  implementation and its result observed; `discovered`: the artifact exists
  and is bound, but was not run here; `declared`: only the link is asserted.
  `opendomain bind` states the depth it audited from, and a VERIFIED record
  without `automation` reads as claimed-versus-actual.
- `binding` — how the `verifies` edge was established: `GENERATED`
  (provisioner tag), `ANNOTATED` (`// odc:<ID>` comment), `ATTRIBUTED`
  (language-native marker), or `INFERRED` (naming convention, LOW
  confidence). An INFERRED binding cannot close a traceability edge until
  `confirmed = true` after human review; the framework never presents the
  origins as equivalent.

## The difference from a unit test

- A **unit test** verifies a function. A **contract test** verifies a boundary
  against its declared schema. A **scenario test** (`SCN`) verifies that
  several correct behaviours compose.
- A test that cannot fail is worse than no test, because it consumes the
  confidence that a real test would provide.

## Rules for this registry

- No test without a `verifies` link. Gate 7 blocks an orphan test: a test that
  verifies nothing is a maintenance liability, not evidence.
- Only mark a test `VERIFIED` after running it. This is the single easiest
  value in the framework to fake, and faking it makes the entire trace
  meaningless.
- Record the tolerance. A test with no tolerance quietly grows one.
- When the implementation under test was executed outside this repository's own
  loop, record where and how it was verified — an out-of-repository claim must
  name the execution that verified it:
  `run = "runs/run-<NNN>-<slug>"` cites an archived run directory, and, when
  the claim rests on one node's verdict, `run-node = "…"` — that node's last
  `gates.log` line is what makes the citation checkable. `opendomain provenance`
  verifies every citation against the archive it names: a citation that names
  no archive is an appeal, not evidence. An archived run is evidence in the
  same sense as this registry — append-only, never rewritten after the fact.

## What an audit is for

An audit answers one question: **can you show that what was built is what was
asked for?** A trail that cannot answer it is not a documentation problem; it
is an accountability problem, and it surfaces at the worst possible time.

## Rules for this registry

- Record the question, not just the verdict. An audit whose scope is not stated
  cannot be re-run.
- An audit that only ever concludes `PASS` is not an audit.
- Accepted unknowns belong here, in writing. The alternative is discovering them
  during the incident.

# Drift

Where the implementation and the specification disagree, `DRIFT-###`. One
artifact per drift.

**Drift is not a failure of discipline to be hidden. It is a fact discovered
and recorded.** The project that files drift honestly can still be wrong; the
project that quietly edits the specification after the code was written has
lost the ability to tell anyone what was agreed.

Required fields: `status`, `type`, `specification`, `implementation`, `decision`.

`type` is one of `OMISSION` `ADDITION` `DIVERGENCE` `REVERSAL`.

`status` is one of `OPEN` `ACCEPTED` `SPEC_UPDATED` `IMPLEMENTATION_UPDATED` `REJECTED`.

## Rules for this registry

- Drift is filed when it is *discovered*, not when it is fixed. An open drift
  record is a live signal; Gate 7 blocks on open drift.
- Say explicitly which side changed and why.
- A drift with a `decision` but no `rationale` is a drift that will be
  relitigated at the worst possible moment.
- When the drift was surfaced while agents were executing the work, cite the
  archived run where it surfaced — with the first-class field
  `run = "runs/run-<NNN>-<slug>"` (and `run-node = "…"` when the claim rests
  on one node's gate line). `opendomain provenance` verifies every citation
  against the archive it names; a citation that names no archive is an
  appeal, not evidence.

## The three failure modes this registry exists for

1. **Each unit is right, the flow is wrong.** Composition is where most defects
   actually live.
2. **The happy path is tested, the exception is not.** Scenarios must include
   at least one failure per critical flow.
3. **Nobody checks the total.** A scenario that only asserts one step is a unit
   test wearing a scenario's clothes.

## Rules for this registry

- A scenario crosses at least two contexts, or it is a test, not a scenario.
- Always include one scenario per critical flow that ends in failure.
- Assert the whole expected result, not just the last step. The "and on-hand
  quantity rises by 15 only" is the part that catches the real bugs.
